'''Quahl''' ({{IPAc-en|k|uː|ɑː|l}} {{respell|k|oo|ah|l}}), formerly known as '''Initiative Q,''' was an attempt to create a new [[payment network]] and [[digital currency]].<ref name="not crypto"/> It was created by [[State of Israel|Israel]]i [[entrepreneur]] [[Saar Wilf]], who previously founded Fraud Sciences, a payment security company acquired by PayPal.<ref name="not crypto"/><ref name="news.com.au"/><ref name="TiA"/><ref name="techcrunch"/> Quahl is backed by [[Cato Institute]] [[economist]] [[Lawrence H. White]].<ref name="news.com.au"/> The initiative has indicated it will not take measures to evade state regulation.<ref name="CUPMedia"/>

==Payment system==
Quahl's goal was to create a new payment system rather than replace payment cards and paper money.<ref name="exame"/><ref name="timesofindia"/> It is "creating a new currency (Quahl) and distributing it to anyone who helps speed up adoption."<ref name="exame"/> Quahl is not a cryptocurrency and is not decentralized,<ref name="exame"/><ref name="stuff"/> but will instead be overseen by an independent monetary committee, similar to a central bank.<ref name="TiA"/><ref name="exame"/>

Since 2018 Quahl was giving away free amounts of Q currency to people who join the network, which is by invite only, and the amount of money drops as more people join the network and will stop on the launch date.<ref name="ftalphaville"/> It has been said that each Q has a value around one US dollar.<ref name="timesofindia"/> "The more people join the network, the more value it has."<ref name="stuff"/>

==Marketing and rollout==
Registering for Quahl is marketed through [[multi-level marketing]].<ref name="portfolio.hu"/> The currency reserved for registrants will not be released until a critical mass of adopters identify themselves.<ref name="TiA"/><ref name="ftalphaville"/> In November 2018, [[Vox.com]] reported that more than two million people had signed up in 180 countries.<ref name="not crypto"/> Later the same month, [[O Globo]] reported more than five million registrations,<ref name="oglobo"/> and [[The Times of India]] reported that countries with large numbers of registrations included India, Brazil, United States and United Kingdom.<ref name="timesofindia"/>

==Criticism==
In October 2018, Frank Chung of [[news.com.au]] wrote that the marketing style could be "perceived as a [[scam]] or [[pyramid scheme]]"<ref name="news.com.au"/> and Daniel Huszák of [[portfolio.hu]] compared it to [[multi-level marketing]] without the fee.<ref name="portfolio.hu"/> Huszák enumerated potential problems with the scheme such as no clear crypto-currency security measures, unclear transaction/[[Foreign exchange market|exchange]] costs, and potential for [[market manipulation]] by the largest holders of currency.<ref name="portfolio.hu" /> Owen Gough of [[Digital Spy]] wrote 
"Is Initiative Q real or fake? Short answer – we have absolutely no idea."<ref name="digitalspy"/>

In contrast, Brendan Markey-Tower, economist at the [[University of Queensland]], said on [[Stuff.co.nz]] in November 2018 that it was "not a scam" and that the scheme wouldn't "make you fabulously wealthy. It is, nonetheless, an interesting idea."<ref name="stuff"/>

==Cessation==
In November 2021, Quahl's main site and app announced the pause of new subscriptions for now as the size of the community (10 million users) and its growth was not sufficient to launch a new currency. It said it was investigating possible ways to move forward in a way that would bring value to the community, and if it did not find a reasonable option, it would delete all user data. As of November 2022 the project is no longer live and all personal information has been permanently erased.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quahl |url=https://quahl.com/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Quahl |language=en |archive-date=2023-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230925223721/https://quahl.com/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>
